The baseline's '38 passed / 2000 ok, 0 failed' existed only as prose; its own report admits the scratch files were cleaned up. Same claim, opposite epistemic status, and nothing in iterations 1-2 could tell them apart.

Eval-1's two baseline failures are both guide-layer and sharper than expected. The baseline left guide/decisions.md and then-vs-now.md byte-identical to the pre-patch fixture, so after the ruling the guide actively CONTRADICTS the specs it projects. A grader confirmed by running the renderer against the patched specs and diffing. Caveat to keep attached to this number: the assertion rewards shipping tooling (the with-skill arm has a renderer, the baseline does not). That is a real property of the skill, not a rigged test, but it should be stated whenever 11/11-vs-9/11 is quoted. In iteration-2 the contaminated baseline hand-edited the guide into drift; sandboxed here it left it stale — two routes to the same defect.

Eval-3 measures the spec's own definition of success (executor consumes the workspace with NO skill in either arm; arms differ only in which workspace they were handed). The executor given the skill-generated workspace booted Postgres, ran the twin-boot harness, found and fixed a real header-casing bug (0/4 -> 4/4, then 8/8), recorded a ledger transition to awaiting_gate_approval, and halted at a gate packet for human sign-off. The executor given the baseline workspace picked the right first task and read specs, but ran out of time waiting on a docker image pull, never ran verification, and — the discriminating gap — left no durable status artifact: with no ledger, the only record of progress sits in a chat fragment OUTSIDE the workspace, so a follow-on session must reconstruct state by git archaeology. Transcript evidence is stark: 32 spec reads vs 1.

KNOWN DEFECT, do not read eval-3's assertion 5 as a result: it asserts specific fidelity behaviors (200-empty-body quirk, async email) that both workspaces deliberately DEFER behind their first work item. A correctly-scoped executor cannot satisfy it, and an executor that ignored its plan would pass it — it rewards what the eval means to penalize. It failed for both arms, so it does not distort the comparison, but rewrite it scope-relative before any future iteration. See ASSERTION-DEFECT.md.

Watch item on the autonomy framing: it tells agents to 'make a defensible choice OR record it as an open question'. The eval-0 baseline used that license to unilaterally decide the slug-collision fix even though the prompt said 'nobody has decided yet'. Framing is identical for both arms so the comparison is fair, but the wording may pull against the open-question assertions — candidate fix: 'record it as an open question; decide only what the task actually delegates to you'.

Scope discipline is a genuine repeated baseline failure, not a technicality: the eval-2 baseline read 'we won't be reachable' as authorization to skip design review entirely and shipped a complete 790-line FastAPI implementation with migrations, tests and Docker, when a workspace was requested. Its analysis was honest and its citations resolved — the failure is instruction-following, not competence.

Cost is the real trade, and the raw token column overstates it (cache reads dominate: 34.6M vs 3.7M is mostly cache). Actual spend: $57.50 with skill vs $9.77 baseline across 8 arms; output tokens 510k vs 165k; wall-clock near-identical (117 vs 111 min) only because arms ran concurrently. Per eval the skill costs ~3-7x. Cheapest case eval-1 ($1.15 vs $0.84, a small spec slice); most expensive eval-0 ($29.02 vs $4.80).

Run integrity, for anyone reading these numbers later: three arms were re-run after dying on 'API Error: Connection closed mid-response' under 8-way concurrency. They were NOT graded-and-discounted — they lost real work (eval-0 with_skill reached 94 turns with no backlog or harness; eval-2 with_skill reached only P4 of 11 phases), so grading them would have UNDERSTATED the skill. Attempts preserved in ../iteration-3-discarded-attempts/. Final runs are all is_error=false and phase-complete. Concurrency now capped at 2.

Two harness bugs fixed this iteration, both of which would have silently corrupted results: (1) copy-back vacuumed up environment rather than work product — a 4,300-file .venv and 2,572 files of Postgres server state; now excluded, with captured traces and boot logs deliberately kept as evidence. (2) grade_checks' eval-3 delta counted .git internals (including Claude Code's own .git/ai/working_logs), which made 'legacy untouched' fail for a run that never edited a legacy file.
n=1 per cell. Direction is consistent across three iterations and two models and the mechanisms are explained rather than inferred, but no single number here has an error bar.
